title: 📘 UNIT 7: GEOGRAPHIC ISSUES AND PUBLIC CONCERNS
notes: Major contemporary geographic concerns are closely related to population dynamics, inequality, resource degradation and human well-being.

title: 👥 7.1 POPULATION-RELATED CONCERNS OF OUR CONTEMPORARY WORLD
notes:
Important population-related concerns include :-

👨‍👩‍👧 Family size
💰 Household income
📚 Education access
📈 Population growth
💹 Economic growth and living standards
💼 Unemployment
🧑‍🔧 Underemployment

⭐ These factors strongly influence household livelihoods and socioeconomic development.

title: 📈 7.1.1 POPULATION GROWTH-RELATED CHALLENGES IN DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
notes:
Developing countries (DCs) have experienced higher population growth than more developed countries (MDCs).

📌 The highest population growth rates in DCs occurred mainly from 1960–1990, while growth rates have generally declined in recent decades.

⚠️ Major challenges :-
🌱 Land degradation and resource depletion
🌳 Biodiversity and habitat loss
🏙️ Rapid urbanization and slum expansion
🍚 Poverty and malnutrition
💧 Food and water insecurity
🏥 Health problems
📚 Limited education access
🚜 Rural–urban migration
🏠 Housing shortages
⚖️ Inequality and marginalization
🌡️ Climate-related hazards
🚌 Transportation shortages

⭐ Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to experience particularly rapid population growth.

title: 🛠️ 7.1.1.1 REMEDIAL MEASURES FOR POPULATION CHALLENGES
notes:
Important strategies include :-

📚 Invest in human capital through education, employment and health services.

👴 Promote healthy aging and economic well-being among older people.

🏙️ Apply sustainable urban planning and provide adequate infrastructure.

🛡️ Strengthen the adaptive capacity of vulnerable populations.

🌍 Promote international cooperation on migration.

🏘️ Strengthen rural–urban relations through integrated development planning.

👩‍🎓 Improve girls' and women's education.

🏥 Increase access to reproductive health services.

⚖️ Ensure equal access to employment and socioeconomic opportunities.

⭐ Population policies should connect demographic change with long-term development.

title: 👨‍👩‍👧 7.1.2 FAMILY SIZE, EDUCATION AND INCOME
notes:
Family :- people connected by kinship, blood relationships or marriage.

🏠 Household :- people living together and sharing food, shelter and other essential needs; members do not necessarily have blood or marriage relationships.

⭐ Relationship among family size, income and education :-
🔹 Large families can divide household income among more members.
🔹 Lower-income households often have larger families.
🔹 Fewer children can allow greater investment per child.
🔹 Higher income can improve nutrition, health and education.
🔹 Education, especially for women, can contribute to lower fertility.

📌 Multi-generational households contain three or more generations living together.
📌 Skipped-generation households contain grandparents and grandchildren without the children's parents.

title: 💰 7.1.2.1 HOUSEHOLD INCOME AND INEQUALITY
notes:
Household income :- earnings received by households or their members in money or useful goods and services.

🌍 Income is unevenly distributed across the world.

⚠️ Low-income households may experience :-
🔹 Poor nutrition
🔹 Limited health services
🔹 Limited education investment
🔹 Greater poverty
🔹 Higher vulnerability to economic shocks

⭐ Income, family size and education influence one another and therefore affect household well-being.

title: 📊 7.1.3 RATES OF POPULATION AND ECONOMIC GROWTH
notes:
Two major contrasting views explain the relationship between population growth and economic development :-

1️⃣ Malthusian and Neo-Malthusian views → population growth can hinder economic progress.

2️⃣ Anti-Malthusian views → population growth can create opportunities for innovation, labour and economic development.

⭐ The relationship is complex and depends on institutions, technology, employment, human capital, resource availability and income distribution.

title: 📉 7.1.3.1 MALTHUSIAN AND NEO-MALTHUSIAN VIEWS
notes:
👤 Thomas Robert Malthus (1766–1834)

Malthus argued that population grows faster than food production.

👥 Population → Geometric progression
1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32...

🍚 Food production → Arithmetic progression

⚠️ Result according to Malthus :-
Population exceeds food supply → scarcity → hunger → disease → conflict/war.

🛑 Preventive checks :- delayed marriage, sexual restraint and fewer children.

Neo-Malthusians similarly emphasize the imbalance between population and economic growth but support family planning as an important preventive measure.

title: 🌱 7.1.3.2 ANTI-MALTHUSIAN VIEWS
notes:
👤 Karl Marx criticized Malthus and argued that poverty and food problems are connected to the organization of production and distribution.

👤 Esther Boserup argued that population growth can encourage agricultural innovation and technological development.

⭐ Boserup's main idea :-
Population pressure → greater food demand → agricultural innovation → increased production.

💡 Key principle :- necessity encourages invention.

📌 Population growth can provide a larger labour force and market, but development requires institutions, policies, human capital and employment opportunities.

title: 💼 7.1.4 UNEMPLOYMENT AND UNDEREMPLOYMENT
notes:
Employment :- participation in income-generating activities that provide money or useful products for livelihood.

Types include :-
🏢 Private employment
🏛️ Public employment
👨‍💼 Self-employment
🧑‍🔧 Temporary or permanent work

Unemployment :- lack of an appropriate occupation for an active working person who wants livelihood support.

Underemployment :- employment in which the amount of work, working time, productivity, skills or payment is below the worker's expectations or capacity.

⭐ Underemployment represents under-utilization of workers' capacities.

title: 📐 7.1.4.1 UNEMPLOYMENT RATE
notes:
Unemployment Rate = (Number of unemployed ÷ Employed + Unemployed) × 100

🇪🇹 Example given for Ethiopia in 2022 :-
Unemployed = 2,350,000
Employed = 56,000,000

Unemployment Rate = 2,350,000 ÷ 58,350,000 × 100 ≈ 4%

⭐ Developing countries often face high unemployment because rapid population growth and urbanization increase job demand faster than economic structures can absorb workers.

title: 👥 7.1.4.2 ECONOMIC DEPENDENCY RATIO
notes:
Economic Dependency Ratio (EDR) relates dependents/non-workers to employed workers.

EDR = (Unemployed + Economically inactive/underemployed + Population aged 0–14) ÷ Employed × 100

🇪🇹 Ethiopia urban population example, 2018 :-
EDR = 149

⭐ Meaning :- approximately 149 dependents could be supported by 100 employed persons in terms of food, clothing, health, education and other needs.

📌 High dependency ratios increase pressure on working populations and household resources.

title: 🌱 7.2 LAND DEGRADATION AND DESERTIFICATION
notes:
Land degradation :- long-term decline in the quality, productivity and ecological integrity of land resources.

It affects :-
🌱 Soil
💧 Water resources
🌳 Vegetation
🐾 Biodiversity
🌾 Agricultural productivity

⭐ Land degradation involves deterioration of physical, chemical and biological processes.

title: 🪨 7.2.1 FORMS OF LAND DEGRADATION
notes:
1️⃣ Physical degradation :- physical breakdown and alteration of land resources.

Examples :-
🔹 Soil compaction
🔹 Crusting
🔹 Hardening
🔹 Thinning
🔹 Sealing
🔹 Changes in soil structure and texture

2️⃣ Chemical degradation :- alteration of chemical components of land resources.

Examples :-
🔹 Nutrient loss
🔹 Soil acidity
🔹 Soil alkalinity
🔹 Eutrophication
🔹 Changes in biomass quality

3️⃣ Biological degradation :- deterioration of biological resources.

Causes :-
🌳 Deforestation
🐄 Overgrazing
🧪 Harmful chemicals

title: ⚠️ 7.2.2 CAUSES OF LAND DEGRADATION
notes:
Natural causes :-
🌋 Volcanic eruptions
🌊 Floods
🌊 Tsunamis

Human causes :-
🌾 Overcropping
🐄 Overgrazing
🌳 Deforestation
🔥 Forest burning
🧪 Pollution
💧 Poor water management
🏗️ Unsustainable land use
👥 Population pressure

⭐ Removal of natural vegetation increases soil erosion and exposes land to degradation.

title: 💥 7.2.3 EFFECTS AND MANAGEMENT OF LAND DEGRADATION
notes:
Effects :-
🌾 Reduced agricultural productivity
💰 Lower household income
🌱 Loss of soil fertility
💧 Water-resource degradation
🐾 Biodiversity loss
🌡️ Greater climate vulnerability
🍚 Food insecurity
💨 Increased greenhouse-gas emissions

Management :-
🌳 Afforestation and reforestation
🚫 Control unsustainable tree cutting
🌾 Avoid expansion of farming into marginal lands
⚡ Use alternative energy sources
🌱 Improve soil management
💧 Improve water management
🐄 Control overgrazing
🌿 Maintain vegetation cover

title: 🏜️ 7.2.4 DESERTIFICATION
notes:
Desertification :- land degradation occurring in dry, arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas.

🌍 Difference :-
Land degradation → can occur in both dry and wet areas.
Desertification → specifically occurs in drylands.

Major human causes :-
👥 Population pressure
🌾 Expansion of farming into drylands
🔥 Forest burning
📋 Poor policies
🌱 Inappropriate land-use practices
🌡️ Human-induced climate change

Characteristics :-
🏜️ Increased aridity
🧂 Saline/barren soils
🌿 Sparse vegetation

title: 🛠️ 7.2.4.1 DESERTIFICATION IMPACTS AND CONTROL
notes:
Impacts :-
🌾 Reduced agricultural productivity
💰 Reduced household income
🌱 Loss of biodiversity
🦠 Expansion of invasive species
🧂 Increased soil salinity
🌡️ Increased greenhouse-gas emissions

Control measures :-
🌾 Dry farming and irrigation
💧 Water harvesting
🌱 Drought-resistant and short-maturing crops
🏞️ Terracing
🌾 Intercropping
🌱 Relay cropping
🚜 Reduced tillage
💼 Livelihood diversification
📢 Early-warning systems
🧠 Indigenous and local knowledge

title: 🏜️ 7.3 RECURRENT DROUGHTS AND FAMINES
notes:
Drought :- prolonged deficiency of moisture and water, commonly associated with rainfall shortage and hydrological imbalance.

Famine :- persistent and severe hunger or starvation caused by food and water scarcity over a geographic area.

⭐ Drought and famine are related but not identical.

Drought → water shortage → crop/livestock losses → food shortage → higher prices and insecurity → possible famine.

title: 🌧️ 7.3.1 TYPES OF DROUGHT
notes:
🌦️ Meteorological drought :- prolonged shortfall of rainfall.

💧 Hydrological drought :- below-normal water flow in lakes, streams and underground water sources.

🌾 Agricultural drought :- insufficient moisture in topsoil for crop growth.

🌍 Environmental drought :- combined effects of meteorological, hydrological and agricultural drought.

💰 Socioeconomic drought :- imbalance between supply and demand of resources such as water, food, fodder, fish and energy.

title: 🌍 7.3.1.1 DROUGHT PATTERNS AND CAUSES
notes:
Droughts are particularly common in arid and dryland regions.

Factors that intensify drought :-
🌡️ High temperatures
🌬️ Hot and dry air masses
☀️ Persistent high-pressure conditions
🌧️ Reduced rainfall
💧 Excessive moisture loss
🌡️ Climate change

📌 Drought frequency and intensity have increased in some regions, including West Africa and the Mediterranean, while some other regions have experienced decreasing trends.

title: 💥 7.3.1.2 IMPACTS OF DROUGHT
notes:
Direct and indirect impacts :-

🌾 Crop failure
🐄 Livestock deaths
💧 Water shortages
🌿 Reduced plant diversity
🐾 Biodiversity loss
🏭 Business disruption
💼 Employment and income losses
🏥 Human and animal health problems
🍚 Food insecurity
📈 Higher food prices
🥣 Malnutrition and famine
📚 School dropout
🚶 Migration
⚠️ Social unrest and conflict

title: 🛡️ 7.3.1.3 DROUGHT RESPONSE AND MITIGATION
notes:
Important measures :-
📡 Improve drought monitoring.
💧 Improve water management.
🌾 Improve crop management.
📢 Increase public awareness and education.
🏞️ Apply watershed management.
🚨 Strengthen early-warning systems.

Soil and water conservation :-
🔹 Crop rotation
🔹 Row cropping
🔹 Terracing
🔹 Minimum tillage
🔹 Trenches
🔹 Shallow wells
🔹 Shelterbelts
🔹 Mulching
🔹 Reclamation of salt-affected soils

🐄 Herd management → control livestock numbers and parasites.

title: 🍚 7.3.2 FAMINE
notes:
Famine is a widespread and severe condition of persistent hunger, malnutrition, starvation, illness and death.

Causes include :-
🏜️ Recurrent drought
🌊 Floods
⛰️ Landslides
🌊 Tsunamis
🦗 Locust invasions
🦠 Epidemics
⚖️ Unequal resource distribution
⚔️ Wars and conflicts
💰 Inequality

⭐ Famine can last from several months to several years.

title: 🛠️ 7.3.2.1 FAMINE PREVENTION AND RESPONSE
notes:
Immediate response :-
🍚 Humanitarian food assistance
🏥 Healthcare
💧 Basic necessities

Long-term measures :-
🏘️ Rebuild affected communities.
🌾 Strengthen local food-system resilience.
💼 Diversify employment and livelihoods.
🏭 Diversify the economy.
🛒 Improve markets and product distribution.

⭐ Food aid can save lives during emergencies, but long-term resilience and economic development are necessary to reduce recurrent famine.

title: 🌳 7.4 DEFORESTATION
notes:
Deforestation :- removal of forest trees and conversion of forest areas through activities such as commercial logging, agricultural expansion, construction and fuel-wood collection.

🌳 Forests provide important services :-
🌡️ Climate regulation
🌊 Flood control
💧 Water regulation
🌱 Soil-erosion control
🌍 Carbon storage
🐾 Wildlife habitat

⭐ Deforestation reduces these ecosystem services.

title: 🔥 7.4.1 CAUSES OF DEFORESTATION
notes:
Underlying causes :-
🌡️ Climate change
👥 Population pressure
🏛️ Government policies
💰 Socioeconomic conditions
🧠 Cultural practices
📋 Weak forest governance

Proximate/direct causes :-
🌾 Clearing and burning forests for farmland
🪵 Fuel-wood collection
🌳 Timber production
🏘️ Settlement expansion
🛣️ Infrastructure development
⛏️ Mining and quarrying
🪓 Commercial logging
🐄 Overstocking and overgrazing

⭐ Underlying causes create the conditions; proximate causes directly remove forest vegetation.

title: 💥 7.4.2 CONSEQUENCES OF DEFORESTATION
notes:
Forest removal can cause :-

🌍 Reduced carbon storage
🐾 Biodiversity loss
🏞️ Destruction of wildlife habitats
💧 Disruption of hydrological cycles
🌊 River ecosystem disruption
🏜️ Increased drought risk
🍚 Increased famine risk
🌧️ Soil erosion
🌊 Flooding
💨 Sedimentation
🌱 Soil nutrient depletion
🌡️ Global warming and climate change

⭐ Deforestation affects both natural ecosystems and human livelihoods.

title: 🌲 7.4.3 DEFORESTATION CONTROL
notes:
Important measures :-
🌳 Afforestation
🌲 Reforestation
🚫 Area closures
🔥 Control forest burning
🪓 Restrict commercial logging
⚡ Use alternative energy instead of firewood
🏭 Use alternative materials instead of timber
🌱 Promote proper forest management

⭐ Sustainable forest management reduces forest loss while maintaining forest resources and ecosystem services.

title: 💻 7.5 WORLDWIDE DIGITAL DIVIDE
notes:
Digital divide :- the gap between people, households, businesses and geographic areas in access to information and communication technologies (ICTs) and the internet.

Important indicators :-
📱 Mobile-phone access
💻 Computer access
📺 Television access
🌐 Internet access
📡 Telecommunication services

⭐ The digital divide can create unequal access to economic, educational and political opportunities.

title: 🌍 7.5.1 CAUSES OF THE DIGITAL DIVIDE
notes:
Major causes include :-

💰 Income and financial limitations
📡 Poor-quality or expensive connections
📚 Low education levels
🧠 Lack of digital literacy
🖥️ Limited access to ICT equipment
❓ Lack of technological knowledge
🎓 Limited opportunities to learn computer skills
🌍 Geographic location
👨‍👩‍👧 Family size
👴 Age
👩 Gender
🗣️ Cultural and linguistic differences

⭐ Income and education are especially important factors separating digital 'haves' and 'have-nots'.

title: ⚠️ 7.5.2 CONSEQUENCES OF THE DIGITAL DIVIDE
notes:
The digital divide can :-

💰 Increase income inequality.
💼 Affect employment opportunities.
📚 Increase educational inequality.
🌍 Widen differences between countries and regions.
🔐 Increase exposure to digital-security risks.

⚠️ Digitalization can also introduce risks such as cybercrime, criminal networks, illegal financial activity, hate speech and fake news.

title: 🚀 7.5.3 OPPORTUNITIES OF DIGITALIZATION
notes:
Digital technology provides opportunities such as :-

🎓 E-learning and affordable educational materials
🏥 Telemedicine
🩺 Medical information and diagnosis
🌦️ Real-time weather information
🌾 Market information for farmers
👨‍🏫 Teacher training
💬 Social networking
✈️ Travel reservations
🌐 Translation services
💳 Financial services for underserved populations
📞 Customer and support services

⭐ Digital access can improve education, healthcare, communication, markets and financial inclusion.

title: 🌐 7.5.4 BRIDGING THE DIGITAL DIVIDE
notes:
Governments and institutions can reduce the digital divide by :-

📡 Expanding affordable telecommunications.
💻 Increasing ICT availability.
📚 Improving digital literacy.
🎓 Providing opportunities to learn computer skills.
💰 Making internet access more affordable.
🏫 Expanding ICT access in schools.
🏥 Developing accessible digital public services.
🤝 Ensuring equal opportunities for underserved populations.

⭐ Accessible and citizen-oriented e-services can help reduce digital inequality.

title: 🧠 UNIT 7 KEY CONCEPTS
notes:
👨‍👩‍👧 Family :- people connected through kinship, blood or marriage.

🏠 Household :- people sharing food, shelter and other essentials, whether related or not.

💼 Employment :- participation in income-generating work.

🚫 Unemployment :- lack of an appropriate occupation for an active worker.

🧑‍🔧 Underemployment :- employment below a person's available capacity, preferred working time, productivity or skill level.

📊 EDR :- ratio of dependents/non-workers to employed workers.

🌱 Land degradation :- long-term decline in land quality, productivity and ecological integrity.

🏜️ Desertification :- land degradation in dry, arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas.

🏜️ Drought :- prolonged deficiency of moisture and water.

🍚 Famine :- severe and prolonged hunger or starvation over a geographic area.

🌳 Deforestation :- removal of forests and conversion of forest land to other uses.

💻 Digital divide :- unequal access to ICTs, internet and related opportunities.

🌳 Afforestation :- establishing forests on land that was not recently forested.

🌲 Reforestation :- re-establishing forests in previously forested areas.

title: ⭐ UNIT 7 QUICK REVISION
notes:
📌 Major concerns of the contemporary world include population pressure, unemployment, land degradation, desertification, drought, famine, deforestation and digital inequality.

📌 Rapid population growth in developing countries can increase pressure on health, education, housing, employment, food, water and environmental resources.

📌 Family size, household income and education are closely interconnected.

📌 Malthus argued that population can grow faster than food production and create scarcity.

📌 Boserup argued that population pressure can encourage agricultural innovation and technological development.

📌 Unemployment means joblessness; underemployment means under-utilization of workers' capacities.

📌 Land degradation can be physical, chemical or biological.

📌 Desertification is land degradation specifically associated with drylands.

📌 Drought has meteorological, hydrological, agricultural, environmental and socioeconomic forms.

📌 Drought can cause crop failure, livestock deaths, water shortages, food insecurity, poverty, migration and conflict.

📌 Famine can result from drought as well as floods, pests, epidemics, inequality, conflicts and other hazards.

📌 Deforestation is driven by both underlying factors and direct/proximate causes.

📌 Deforestation causes biodiversity loss, habitat destruction, erosion, flooding, nutrient depletion and increased climate-change risks.

📌 Digital divide means unequal access to ICTs and the internet.

📌 Income, education, infrastructure, geography and digital literacy strongly influence the digital divide.

📌 Digitalization can improve education, healthcare, agriculture, communication and financial services.

⭐ Core idea :- Population, economic, environmental and technological issues are interconnected. Sustainable development requires improving livelihoods and access to opportunities while protecting land, forests, water and other resources.
